Source. While `decodeHeader()` iterates nested ASF objects, `HeaderReader` consumes the next 24-byte object header from attacker data. In the staged witness this header starts at offset `0x3c`, yielding GUID=`Stream_Properties` and declared size `0`; earlier object iterations are collapsed here because they only position the cursor at this nested object.

Present but insufficient guard. After step 1, `objectHeader.getSize()` is `0` and `io_->tell()` is 84 in a 96-byte file, so this check sees `0 <= 12` and admits the object. It validates only the advertised object size, not whether `streamProperties()` can still read its own 16-byte GUID payload.

The object GUID parsed at step 1 resolves through `GUIDReferenceTags.find(GUIDTag(objectHeader.getId().data()))` to `Stream_Properties`, so the known-tag branch calls `streamProperties()` directly. Because this is a handled tag, `decodeBlock()` does not enter the unknown/unhandled fallback that requires `remaining_size > 0` before seeking away.
Root cause. `streamProperties()` requests a 16-byte stream-type GUID from the object payload using the partial-read overload; at this point only 12 bytes remain in the file.

The in-memory file backend computes `readCount` from the bytes still available. With `rcount == GUID == 16` but only 12 bytes left after the nested object header, it returns `readCount == 12` and shrinks the `DataBuf` to logical size 12. ASan's allocation stack points to this function as the creator of the short buffer.

Before any size check, `streamProperties()` passes the short buffer to `GUIDTag`, whose constructor assumes a full 16-byte GUID. The later `if (tag_stream_type != GUIDReferenceTags.end())` guard is evaluated only after that constructor returns.

Sink. This final copy reads the last 8 GUID bytes from `bytes[8..15]`. Because step 5 shortened the returned `DataBuf` to 12 bytes, offsets 12..15 lie past its logical end and AddressSanitizer reports the observed `heap-buffer-overflow READ of size 8` here.
